title: Final Prices With a Special Discount in a Shop
description: Brute force to optimized: a forward scan per item versus a single monotonic non-decreasing stack pass that resolves every discount at once.

sections.title: Final Prices With a Special Discount in a Shop

content.title: Final Prices With a Special Discount in a Shop

blocks.text: You are given an integer array prices where prices[i] is the price of the i-th item in a shop. There is a special discount: for each item i, if there exists a LATER item j (j > i) such that prices[j] <= prices[i], the FIRST such item's price is subtracted from prices[i] as the discount. If no such item exists, no discount is applied. Return an array of the FINAL prices after applying every item's discount.

blocks.caption: A monotonic non-decreasing stack of "waiting" indices directly resolves each item's discount in a single pass

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of item prices"],["Output","An array of the same length, with each item's discount (if any) already applied"],["Goal","Find, for every item, the FIRST later item whose price is <= it, in a single linear pass"],["Constraints","1 <= prices.length <= 500; 1 <= prices[i] <= 10^3"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"First later element that is <= (or >=) the current one\" for MANY positions at once","The classic monotonic stack technique, here using a non-decreasing stack (looking for the first SMALLER-OR-EQUAL element, the mirror image of \"next greater element\")"],["Only the discount subtraction (not the raw next-smaller value) is needed","Once found, directly compute and store prices[i] - prices[j] rather than just recording the found value"]]}

blocks.text: This is a "next SMALLER-OR-EQUAL element" problem in disguise: for each item, its discount is defined as the price of the first later item that is not more expensive, and the final price is simply the original price minus that discount (or unchanged, if no such later item exists).

blocks.title: Analogy: A Store's Automatic Price-Match Promotion
blocks.text: Imagine a store where each price tag has an automatic promotion: "if any LATER item on the shelf is priced the same or cheaper, subtract that later price from mine." Walking down the shelf while keeping track of items still "waiting" for such a match, the moment a cheap-enough item appears, it immediately resolves the promotion for every waiting item that it qualifies for.

blocks.caption: The stack holds items still waiting for a later same-or-cheaper price; a new low price resolves the discount for everyone qualifying on top

blocks.text: Before scanning forward from scratch for EACH item (redundant, repeated work), notice this is exactly the "next greater element" pattern, mirrored: a monotonic NON-DECREASING stack finds the first later same-or-cheaper price for every item simultaneously.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "First later item with price <= current" is the mirror image of the classic "next greater element" problem, which uses a monotonic DECREASING stack; here, a monotonic NON-DECREASING stack (of indices, from bottom to top) is the natural analogue.

Observation 2: Walking left to right, maintaining a stack of indices still WAITING for a same-or-cheaper price later on: whenever a new price arrives that is <= the stack's top price, that new price IS the discount for the top (and possibly more entries below it too).

Observation 3: Repeatedly popping and resolving while the stack's top price is still >= the new price correctly handles a single new arrival resolving MULTIPLE waiting items at once.

Observation 4: Anything still left on the stack after the full scan never found a qualifying later price, so those items keep their original price unchanged.
This is the "next smaller-or-equal element" variant of the classic monotonic stack technique, resolving every item's discount simultaneously in a single linear pass.
For each item, scan forward through every later item until the first one with a price less than or equal to it is found, then apply that discount.

items: For each index i, scan every index j > i in order.
The first j found with prices[j] <= prices[i] determines the discount; apply it and stop scanning for that i.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop directly implements the definition: the FIRST later item satisfying the price condition, stopping the scan as soon as it is found.
This correctly handles items with no qualifying discount, since the inner loop simply completes without applying any change.

blocks.text: Correctly finds each item's discount, since it directly scans exactly as the problem's definition requires.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case (for example, a strictly decreasing price array, where every scan goes all the way to the very next item).
Space: O(1) extra (excluding the output).
Limitation: repeating a forward scan for every single item is wasteful; a single monotonic stack pass resolves ALL items' discounts simultaneously.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans forward for every item independently. Instead, walk through prices ONCE, maintaining a monotonic non-decreasing stack of indices still waiting for their discount. Whenever a new price is <= the stack's top price, pop and apply that new price as the discount for the popped index, repeating until the stack's top is no longer >= the new price.

Walk through prices with a stack of indices. For each index i: while the stack is non-empty and prices[stack top] >= prices[i], pop that index and set its result to prices[popped index] - prices[i]. Push i. Indices remaining on the stack at the end keep their original, unchanged price.
Use a monotonic non-decreasing stack of indices to resolve every item's discount in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The results are [4,2,4,2,3], matching the expected output.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n): each index is pushed and popped at most once.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

Each index pushed onto the stack represents "an item still waiting for a same-or-cheaper price further ahead." The moment such a price arrives, it is guaranteed to be the FIRST (nearest) qualifying price for every waiting index still sitting on top of the stack, since anything even cheaper appearing earlier would have already resolved them. Popping and resolving repeatedly correctly handles one new arrival resolving multiple waiting items at once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A new price is <= the stack's top price","Pop and apply the discount, possibly repeating for multiple items below it"],["A new price is strictly greater than the stack's top","Simply pushed, joining the \"waiting\" indices"],["Indices remain on the stack after the full scan","Those items never found a qualifying discount, keeping their original price"]]}

items: Storing INDICES (not prices) on the stack allows directly updating the correct position in the result array once a discount is resolved.
The while loop's condition (prices[stack top] >= prices[i], using >=, not >) correctly matches the problem's "same or cheaper" (<=) discount condition.
The result array starts as a copy of the original prices, so indices never resolved simply keep their unchanged value automatically.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (forward scan per item)","O(n^2)","O(1) extra","Repeats scanning work across every item"],["Optimized (monotonic non-decreasing stack)","O(n)","O(n)","Resolves every item's discount simultaneously in one pass"]]}

blocks.text: "First later element that is <= (or >=) the current one," asked for every position in an array, is the mirror-image signal of the classic monotonic stack "next greater element" pattern, solvable identically with a non-decreasing (rather than decreasing) stack.

items: Using a strict > instead of >= in the stack's pop condition, which would miss cases where a later price is EXACTLY equal (the problem explicitly allows equal prices to qualify for the discount).
Storing prices directly on the stack instead of indices, losing the ability to update the correct position in the result array.
Rescanning forward for each item individually, missing the opportunity to resolve all items in a single combined pass.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Strictly increasing prices","No item ever finds a qualifying discount, so the result equals the original array"],["Strictly decreasing prices","Every item (except the last) finds its discount immediately (the very next item)"],["Multiple equal prices in a row","Each earlier equal price is discounted down to 0 by the very next equal price, since <= includes equality"]]}

items: Explicitly framing this as "next smaller-or-equal element" and connecting it to the more commonly known "next greater element" pattern demonstrates strong pattern transfer.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the first LATER element that is smaller than (or equal to) the current one, for many positions" points directly to a monotonic non-decreasing stack.

items: How would this change if the discount used the STRICTLY smaller condition instead of smaller-or-equal? Simply change the stack's pop condition from >= to > (a strict inequality), and equal prices would no longer trigger a discount against each other.

How is this related to Daily Temperatures elsewhere in this category? Daily Temperatures finds the next STRICTLY GREATER element (a decreasing stack); this problem finds the next SMALLER-OR-EQUAL element (a non-decreasing stack), the natural mirror image.

What is the maximum possible stack size during the algorithm, and when does it occur? Up to n, when prices are in strictly increasing order (every item keeps waiting, since nothing ever qualifies to resolve it).
A "next smaller-or-equal element" mirror of the classic monotonic stack pattern used in Next Greater Element I and Daily Temperatures elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (monotonic non-decreasing stack): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic non-decreasing stack for "next smaller-or-equal element"
Core Idea: Resolve every item's discount simultaneously using a single stack pass; a new same-or-cheaper price resolves the discount for every waiting item still on top of the stack
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: This is the mirror image of "next greater element": use >= instead of > when popping, since equal prices also qualify for the discount
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Monotonic non-decreasing stack; a same-or-cheaper arrival resolves every waiting item's discount
